blocks.title: Connect objects through explicit responsibilities
paragraphs: Composition represents a has-a relationship using references to collaborators or contained objects. Library types can provide storage and operations, but their contracts still determine what a program may safely assume.

blocks.title: Model relationship meaning before choosing a collection
paragraphs: A Session can refer to one Facilitator and a list of Participants. The relationship describes which objects are connected; an ArrayList is one possible implementation of the many-valued association. Choose fields according to ownership and multiplicity rather than copying every relationship into every object.

A reference does not itself imply exclusive ownership. If two Sessions reference one Facilitator, changes to that shared object may be visible from both. Decide where responsibilities belong and whether a caller may mutate an internal participant collection.

blocks.title: Read the method contract, not just its name
paragraphs: Use documentation to check the parameter types, result, preconditions, effects and exceptional cases. ArrayList.get(index) requires a valid existing index; adding at size is permitted, but getting at size is not. A method may return information about the removed or replaced value.

Overloads can have different meanings: remove(int index) removes by position, while remove(Object value) removes a matching object. With a list of Integer values, argument type affects which overload is selected. Read the exact signature before using an integer literal.

blocks.title: A library abstraction is not a promise of zero cost
paragraphs: ArrayList grows as needed, but growing its backing storage may copy elements. Inserting or removing near the front shifts later elements. Do not claim that every addition has constant cost; choose an API based on the required behavior and the scale of the task.

Document your own public methods with the same discipline: accepted inputs, observable changes, outputs and failure behavior. A caller should not need your implementation to discover whether an operation mutates its arguments.

blocks.title: Apply indexed-list contracts in sequence
paragraphs: Insertion at index1 places dusk between dawn and noon. remove(0) removes and returns dawn; the remaining first entry is dusk and the size is2. This example uses String elements so the index-removal overload is unambiguous.

blocks.title: Choose a relationship, then honor the API
paragraphs: First draw the object relationships and identify who owns each responsibility. Then select a library representation, read its contracts and decide how much mutable internal state callers may access.

cards.prompt: How is a has-a relationship different from an is-a relationship?
cards.answer: Composition connects an object to another object it uses or contains. Inheritance claims a subtype can act as the more general type. Having a collection does not make an object a subtype of that collection.

cards.prompt: Does a many-valued association force an ArrayList implementation?
cards.answer: No. Multiplicity states how many related objects there can be. The representation also depends on required order, duplicates, lookup and mutation behavior.

cards.prompt: What should you inspect in an API entry before calling a method?
cards.answer: The exact signature, parameter meaning, return value, preconditions, side effects and exceptional cases. A familiar method name alone does not establish its behavior.

cards.prompt: For List<Integer> values, why can values.remove(1) differ from values.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))?
cards.answer: The int argument selects index removal; the Integer argument selects object removal. One removes the element at position1, while the other removes a matching value if present.

guided.title: Design a session roster around documented APIs
guided.prompt: A Session has one facilitator and an ordered roster of unique participant names. Design its fields, enroll(name) and a way to inspect names. Decide whether a caller can mutate the internal roster. Explain which List operations you need and their contracts.

fields.label: Read-only observation or copying policy and API checks

rubric: Represents a single facilitator and a many-valued roster without an inheritance claim.
Defines duplicate and order behavior explicitly.
Does not accidentally expose the internal mutable list through its observation method.
Uses documented contains/add/get or copy behavior with valid index assumptions.
reference: One design stores a Facilitator reference and a private List<String>. enroll checks the stated name precondition and contains(name) before appending; it returns whether the roster changed.

Return a new ArrayList<>(names) if callers may mutate their returned list independently, or provide narrow indexed queries. These alternatives have different interfaces but can satisfy the same ownership goal.

The list copy separates outer-list mutation. For immutable String elements, sharing each element reference does not expose mutable name state. State that reasoning rather than claiming every list copy is a deep copy.
